It is late, so I'll keep this short. Before you close the notes, there are two errors in what I gave you:

1. **COBIT:** I wrote "COBIT 2019 (and its successor, COBIT 2019 with updates)," which makes no sense. COBIT 2019 is the current version. It has had supplementary publications, but no successor.
2. **ITIL access management:** I listed "Access management" as an ITIL 4 practice, but it isn't one of the 34. It was a formal process in ITIL v3. In ITIL 4, access is handled mainly through **Information security management** and **Service request management**. Also, "Deployment and release management" is really two separate practices, Deployment management and Release management.

The COBIT mapping for patching (BAI03) is also loose. BAI03 is about solution build, so BAI06 (changes) and DSS05 (security services) fit better.

The overall conclusion still holds: ISO/IEC 27001 is the certifiable option, and the others support it. Get some sleep!

# ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Gap-Analysis Checklist: Mid-Sized Fintech (AWS, Entra ID, Terraform, JSM)

**Caveats:** I'm inferring likely gaps from your description, so validate each against what you actually have. "Azure AD" is now **Microsoft Entra ID**, which auditors will expect in your documentation. Because you process payments, **PCI DSS** probably applies and overlaps heavily with this list. Your financial regulator's requirements (which depend on jurisdiction) belong in the legal register under 5.31.

**Effort key:** **QW** = quick win (days to ~4 weeks). **PRJ** = project (2+ months, needs planning and owners).

---

## Priority 0: ISMS Clauses 4-10 (mandatory, not Annex A)

Certification bodies fail organizations on these more often than on technical controls, and "no formal ISMS" means this is likely your biggest gap.

| Requirement | Likely gap | Evidence examples | Effort |
|---|---|---|---|
| Scope, context, interested parties (Cl. 4) | Scope undefined | Scope statement (e.g., "payments API platform, supporting AWS accounts, and staff"), interested-parties register | **QW** |
| Leadership, roles, policy (Cl. 5) | No ISMS owner or top-management commitment | Signed information security policy, ISMS roles, steering committee minutes | **QW** |
| Risk methodology, register, treatment plan (Cl. 6.1) | Ad hoc risk handling | Documented methodology, risk register with owners, treatment plan, risk acceptance sign-offs | **PRJ** |
| Statement of Applicability (6.1.3) | Doesn't exist | SoA listing all 93 controls with include/exclude, justification, status | **PRJ** (after risk assessment) |
| Objectives, competence, documented information (Cl. 6.2, 7) | Informal | Measurable objectives, training records, document control in Confluence or SharePoint | **QW** |
| Internal audit, management review, corrective action (Cl. 9-10) | None | Audit program and report, management review minutes, nonconformity log in Jira | **PRJ** |

---

## Priority 1: Foundations and gating controls

| Annex A | Control | Likely gap | Evidence examples | Effort |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5.1, 5.2, 5.4, 5.37 | Policies, roles, procedures | Policies exist but aren't approved, versioned, or communicated | Approved policy set with owners and review dates, acknowledgment records | **QW** |
| 5.31, 5.36 | Legal and regulatory requirements | No consolidated register | Register of regulatory, contractual, and PCI obligations, with owner and control mapping | **QW** |
| 5.9, 5.11 | Asset inventory | Partial CMDB | AWS Config/Resource Explorer export, tagging standard (owner, environment, data class), SaaS inventory | **PRJ** (QW: tag policy plus SaaS list) |
| 5.12, 5.13 | Classification and labeling | Likely none | 3-4 level scheme, data-flow diagram showing where cardholder or customer data lives | **QW** |
| 5.19-5.22 | Supplier security (MSPs, SaaS) | Weak or missing due diligence, SLAs, and monitoring | Supplier register with criticality tiers, security clauses in MSP contracts, SOC 2/ISO reports reviewed, annual review records | **PRJ** (QW: register and tiering) |
| 5.23 | Cloud services security | Shared-responsibility not documented | AWS account structure (Organizations, SCPs), cloud security standard, shared-responsibility matrix | **PRJ** |
| 8.2, 8.5, 5.15-5.18 | Access control, authentication, privileged access | Inconsistent MFA, standing admin rights, no access reviews | Conditional Access policies enforcing MFA, PIM/JIT for admins, IAM Identity Center federation, no long-lived IAM keys, root MFA, quarterly access review sign-offs, joiner/mover/leaver tickets in JSM | **PRJ** (QW: MFA everywhere, remove stale accounts) |

---

## Priority 2: Core technical and operational controls (auditors will sample these)

| Annex A | Control | Likely gap | Evidence examples | Effort |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8.8 | Vulnerability management | Periodic scanning but no SLAs or tracking | Severity-based remediation SLAs, findings tracked in Jira, scan and pen test reports with closure evidence | **QW** (formalize process) |
| 8.9 | Configuration management | Terraform in place, but baselines and drift unmanaged | Hardened baselines (CIS), drift detection, policy-as-code (Checkov, AWS Config rules), state file access controls | **PRJ** |
| 8.32, 8.19 | Change management | Process may not be consistently followed | JSM change records linked to Git PRs, branch protection, required approvals, emergency change procedure | **QW** |
| 5.24-5.28, 6.8 | Incident management | Plan may be informal, with no exercises | IR plan, severity matrix, runbooks, tabletop exercise report, post-incident reviews, staff reporting channel | **PRJ** (QW: IR plan and tabletop) |
| 8.15-8.17 | Logging, monitoring, clock sync | Datadog in place, but retention, coverage, and alert ownership unclear | CloudTrail/VPC flow logs centralized, retention policy, alert rules mapped to use cases, on-call records, protected log storage | **QW** |
| 8.13, 8.14, 5.29, 5.30 | Backup, redundancy, continuity | Backups exist but restores are untested | Backup configs, restore test results, defined RTO/RPO, BC/DR plan, DR exercise report | **PRJ** |
| 8.24 | Cryptography | Likely no key management policy | Crypto standard (TLS versions, algorithms), KMS key policies and rotation, secrets management (Secrets Manager/Vault) | **QW** |
| 8.20-8.22 | Network security | MSP-managed, so you may lack visibility or evidence | VPC/security group reviews, segmentation diagrams, MSP-supplied firewall rule reviews, WAF configs for APIs | **PRJ** |
| 8.1, 8.7 | Endpoints and malware | Coverage gaps (BYOD, contractors) | MDM enrollment reports, EDR coverage, disk encryption status, patch compliance | **QW** to **PRJ** |

---

## Priority 3: Secure development (a key area for an API-based payments company)

| Annex A | Control | Likely gap | Evidence examples | Effort |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8.25-8.29 | SDLC, security requirements, secure coding, testing | Security checks not systematic | Secure SDLC policy, threat models for critical APIs, SAST/SCA/DAST in CI, code review rules, pen test remediation | **PRJ** |
| 8.4 | Source code access | Overly broad repo permissions | Repo access reviews, SSO/MFA on Git platform, secrets scanning | **QW** |
| 8.31, 8.33 | Environment separation, test data | Production data possibly used in test | Separate AWS accounts per environment, data masking or synthetic data procedure | **PRJ** |
| 8.30 | Outsourced development | Contractors or agencies lack clear requirements | Contract clauses, access controls, code review of contractor output | **QW** |
| 5.8 | Security in project management | Security reviews ad hoc | Security checkpoint in project or epic templates | **QW** |

---

## Priority 4: People, physical, and remaining controls

| Annex A | Control | Likely gap | Evidence examples | Effort |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6.1-6.6 | Screening, terms, discipline, NDAs, offboarding | HR process may not cover security | Background check records (as legally allowed), contract security clauses, offboarding checklist | **QW** |
| 6.3 | Awareness training | Not regular or tracked | Onboarding and annual training completion reports, phishing simulation results, role-based training for developers | **QW** |
| 6.7, 7.7 | Remote working, clear desk and screen | Policy gaps | Remote working policy, screen lock enforced via MDM | **QW** |
| 7.1-7.14 | Physical security | Cloud-first, so mostly office-focused | Office access logs, visitor log, media disposal records. Datacenter controls can be justified in the SoA by relying on AWS attestations | **QW** |
| 5.5-5.7 | Authorities, special interest groups, threat intel | Typically absent | Regulator contact list, threat feed subscriptions (e.g., ISAC, vendor advisories) | **QW** |
| 5.10, 5.14 | Acceptable use, information transfer | Policy gaps | AUP acknowledgments, secure transfer standards (SFTP, encrypted email) | **QW** |
| 8.10-8.12, 5.33, 5.34 | Deletion, masking, DLP, records, privacy | Retention and deletion not enforced | Retention schedule, S3 lifecycle rules, deletion logs, DLP rules on email and cloud, privacy register | **PRJ** |
| 5.35 | Independent review | None | Internal audit by an independent person or an external consultant | **PRJ** (ties to Cl. 9) |

---

## Suggested sequencing

**Weeks 0-6 (quick wins):** Define scope, name an ISMS owner, secure management sign-off, build the legal register, supplier register, data classification scheme, and approved policy set, enforce MFA, formalize vulnerability SLAs, and write the IR plan.

**Months 2-5 (core projects):** Run the risk assessment and produce the SoA, clean up access (PIM, reviews), improve asset inventory and supplier due diligence, and run a restore test and an IR tabletop. Add SDLC security gates to CI.

**Months 5-8 (proving it works):** Run internal audit and management review, close nonconformities, and engage a certification body for Stage 1, followed by Stage 2.

Most organizations your size need roughly 6-12 months, mainly because the ISMS needs to show a period of operation (records of reviews, audits, and exercises actually happening).

---

## Practical tips

- **Keep scope tight at first.** Scoping to the payments platform and supporting corporate IT is more manageable than "the whole company."
- **Your MSPs are in scope as suppliers.** Auditors will ask for contracts, SLAs, and evidence you monitor them.
- **Automate evidence.** Terraform, Jira, Datadog, and Entra reports can generate most of what auditors request. Consider a compliance automation tool if you want continuous collection, though it isn't required.
- **Align with PCI DSS and your regulator** in one control framework to avoid triple the work.

# ISMS Tracker, Refined Scope, and Top 10 Quick Wins

## 1. Refined scope statement

Your draft is a good start. The main gaps are the missing supporting tooling, people, devices, locations, and the interfaces to excluded areas, which Clause 4.3 requires you to address.

> **ISMS Scope (v0.1 draft)**
>
> [Company name]'s ISMS covers the design, development, deployment, operation, and support of the **Payments API platform**, which processes payment transactions for customers.
>
> **In scope:**
> - The Payments API platform and its production and pre-production environments, hosted in the associated AWS accounts, including infrastructure managed as code (Terraform)
> - CI/CD pipelines, source code repositories, and artifact and secrets management
> - Identity and access services (Microsoft Entra ID and federated access to AWS and in-scope applications)
> - Operational tooling used to run and secure the platform (Datadog, Jira Service Management, CMDB)
> - Employees and contractors with access to in-scope systems, and the end-user devices they use
> - [Office location(s)] and remote working
> - Third parties: MSPs providing networking and security services, with AWS and SaaS providers managed as suppliers
>
> **Excluded:** corporate HR systems and marketing SaaS, provided they do not store, process, or transmit in-scope information or provide a privileged access path to in-scope systems.
>
> **Interfaces and dependencies:** the HR joiner/mover/leaver feed to Entra ID, AWS shared-responsibility boundaries, and MSP-operated controls are within the ISMS as interfaces.
>
> Applicable standard: ISO/IEC 27001:2022.

**Points to decide before finalizing:**
1. **Dev/test environments.** You listed prod and pre-prod only. If developers use dev/test accounts holding source code, secrets, or production-derived data, include them.
2. **HR exclusion.** Excluding the HR *systems* is fine, but HR *processes* (screening, onboarding, offboarding, terms of employment) still apply to in-scope staff. Auditors will ask how leavers lose access.
3. **Corporate IT.** Entra ID covers all staff, so the corporate laptops and SaaS used to reach in-scope systems will probably be pulled in anyway.
4. **PCI DSS.** If you handle cardholder data, align this scope with your PCI cardholder data environment so you maintain one boundary.
5. **Exclusion justification.** Document why each exclusion doesn't affect your ability to meet security requirements. Auditors check this.

---

## 2. Tracker (CSV, ready to paste)

- Severities are *my assumptions* from your description. Validate each one against reality before assigning work.
